To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the swimming trajectories of bluegills are much more complex in the field than in recirculating flow tunnels and 2) these trajectories are much less variable than the trajectories of volitional swimming behaviors used to predict field locomotor cost.

field swimming trajectories of bluegills are variable and nonlinear, but less unsteady than volitional laboratory swimming behaviors, and field swimming performance data suggest that speed and path‐curvature data can be used to derive estimates of locomotor performance that fit within measured metabolic capacities for activity.

the swimming trajectories and performance of bluegills in the field are more complex than those observed in the laboratory, but that the field performance of these fish is consistent with the capacity for sustainable activity.

understanding the physiological basis for the ability of fish to swim in their natural habitats.
understanding the costs of locomotor activity in the field, which can dominate daily energy expenditures.
quantifying locomotion and its physiological costs in aquatic organisms, with an emphasis on the bluegill sun fish.

the swimming behavior of bluegills in a lake was not steady, but was highly variable in speed and path curvature, and was not consistent with a model of volitional swimming.

the field swimming performance of blue gills was much more variable and unsteady than the steady state swimming performance in recirculating flow channels, and the field swimming performance was less unsteady than volitional swimming behaviors.

the field is a better place to measure the cost of swimming than the laboratory.

The main takeaway from our work is that

field swimming performance of blue gills is highly variable and nonlinear in the field, yet it is much less variable and unsteady than the voluntary swimming behaviors that underlay current predictive models of field locomotor cost.
